'''Andrea Mikhailovich Razmadze''' (sometimes spelled Andria/Andrei Razmadze, 12 August 1889 &ndash; 2 October 1929<ref name="dedication" />) was a Georgian mathematician, and one of the founders of [[Tbilisi State University]], whose Mathematics Institute was renamed in his honor in 1944.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://rmi.tsu.ge/eng/about.htm|website=Andrea Razmadze Mathematical Institute|title=About|accessdate=20 July 2016}}</ref> The department's scientific journal, published continuously since 1937, was also renamed as the [[Proceedings of A. Razmadze Mathematical Institute]] in his honor.

==Biography==
Andrea Razmadze was the son of Mikhail Gavrilovich Razmadze, a railway worker, and Nino Georgievna Nodia.<ref name=Yousch>{{cite web|last1=Youschkevitch|first1=A. P.|title=Razmadze, Andrei Mikhailovich|url=http://www.encyclopedia.com/doc/1G2-2830903600.html|website=www.encyclopedia.com|accessdate=20 July 2016}}</ref> He graduated from [[Kutaisi]] nonclassical secondary school in 1906 (where Public School #41 has been renamed for him<ref>{{cite book|title=Kutaisi Regional Selection Conference|date=2015|publisher=European Youth Parliament|location=Georgia|page=8|url=https://issuu.com/eyp-georgia/docs/krsc_-_info_booklet|accessdate=20 July 2016}}</ref>), then studied at [[Moscow State University|Moscow University]], earning a Diploma in 1910, and then a Masters in 1917 while teaching at local classical and secondary schools.<ref name=CV>{{cite web|title=A. Razmadze. Curriculum Vitae|url=http://rmi.tsu.ge/person/razmadze/|website=A. Razmadze Mathematical Institute|accessdate=20 July 2016}}</ref> At the invitation of the university, he briefly stayed in Moscow University to teach mathematics in 1917,<ref>{{cite book|title=Russian Mathematical Surveys|date=1966|publisher=London Mathematical Society|pages=87–88|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xrTxAAAAMAAJ|language=en}}</ref> but soon left to become one of the founders of Tbilisi University.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Mikaberidze|first1=Alexander|title=Historical Dictionary of Georgia|publisher=Rowman & Littlefield|isbn=9781442241466|pages=550–551|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JNNQCgAAQBAJ|language=en}}</ref> Though he died just 11 years later, during his time there he greatly expanded Georgian mathematical terminology by publishing three textbooks in that language,<ref name=Yousch /> and insisting that all courses be taught in Georgian, an approach that attracted renowned mathematician [[Nikoloz Muskhelishvili]] to the school.<ref name="Maugin">{{cite book|last1=Maugin|first1=Gerard A.|title=Continuum Mechanics Through the Twentieth Century: A Concise Historical Perspective|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=9789400763531|page=189|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-QhAAAAAQBAJ|language=en}}</ref> He also founded the [[Georgian Mathematical Union]] on 21 February 1923 and was its first president; this institution lapsed on his death, but was reorganized from 1962 to the present.<ref>{{cite web|title=GMU - About Us|url=http://www.rmi.ge/~gmu/E_About%20us.htm|website=www.rmi.ge|accessdate=20 July 2016}}</ref> He is most famous for his work in the [[calculus of variations]], where he discovered an efficient method for finding the extrema of integral functions, and a comprehensive theory for finding the extrema of discontinuous ("angular") functions that can be represented by a finite number of curves.<ref name=Yousch /> He presented this last result at the 1924 International Congress of Mathematicians in Toronto,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Razmadze|first1=Andrea M.|title=Sur les solutions discontinues dans le calcul des variations|journal=Mathematische Annalen|date=1925|volume=94|pages=1–52|doi=10.1007/bf01208643|url=http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1924.1/Main/icm1924.1.0561.0588.ocr.pdf}}</ref> for which he was awarded a Sc.D. by the [[University of Paris|Sorbonne]].<ref name="CV"/> He also delivered lectures in [[Jacques Hadamard]]'s famous seminar series in Paris, along with such notables as [[Paul Lévy (mathematician)|Paul Lévy]], [[Laurent Schwartz]], and [[Nobel Prize|Nobel]] laureates [[Louis de Broglie]] and [[Max Born]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Mazʹja|first1=Vladimir G.|last2=Shaposhnikova|first2=T. O.|title=Jacques Hadamard: A Universal Mathematician|date=1999|publisher=American Mathematical Soc.|isbn=9780821819234|page=172|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=F-YN_yOkaNAC|language=en}}</ref>
